Sitefile language draft v0.1

Line-oriented, Dockerfile-inspired, case-insensitive instruction keywords. Quoted strings, comments, and backslash continuations. No implicit shell.

Instructions:

  • FROM scratch|<local dir>|<stage> [AS name]
  • ARG NAME[: type] [= value] external build parameter
  • LET NAME = value local immutable binding
  • IMPORT name FROM <uri> [AS json|text|tree|file] [INTEGRITY sha256:<hex>]
  • COPY [--from=<stage>] <source> <destination>; source can be local path or name:/path
  • RENDER <template> TO <destination>; interpolation ${NAME} only in MVP
  • EXPORT <tree-path> [AS directory|zip|tar|tgz|wbn|oci] [BASE <https-url>] [AT </srv/www>] (CLI specifies destination)
  • PLUGIN, TOOL and TRANSFORM (custom renderers and allow-listed external programs): see Plugins below.
  • Future: REMOVE, GENERATE, ASSERT, META, EXEC.

Path rules: absolute destinations are virtual artifact paths; relative local sources resolve from project context. No implicit archive extraction. No implicit remote COPY in MVP (use IMPORT then COPY). Distinguish file and directory copying; specify trailing slash semantics with tests.

Variables: ARG is externally configurable; LET is local. Missing required values are errors. Escaping is explicit; initial renderer is for text, not automatically HTML-safe.

Example:

FROM scratch
ARG TITLE = "Hello"
COPY ./public/ /
RENDER ./templates/index.html TO /index.html
EXPORT / AS directory

Design decisions still open: typed expression grammar, override syntax, template engine extension API, lockfile format.

v0.1 implementation decisions

These pin down what the draft above leaves open. Tests cover each rule.

Lexical rules

  • One instruction per logical line. A physical line ending in an odd number of \ continues onto the next line; the pieces are joined with one space. Whitespace around the join is trimmed, even inside quotes. Blank lines inside a continuation are skipped; a \ on the last line just ends the instruction.
  • A line whose first non-blank character is # is a comment, also inside a continuation. # elsewhere is ordinary text (URLs contain #).
  • Flags (--overwrite, --escape=…) come before operands. Unknown or repeated flags are syntax errors.
  • Value words (ARG/LET types, IMPORT AS kinds, --escape values, AS directory) are case-insensitive. Only the bare word scratch (not "scratch") means an empty base.
  • INTEGRITY must be a literal lowercase sha256:<64 hex>.
  • Keywords (FROM, AS, TO, INTEGRITY, …) are case-insensitive. Names are case-sensitive identifiers: [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*.
  • An operand is a bare word (up to whitespace), a "double-quoted" string, or a 'single-quoted' string.
    • Bare and double-quoted text interpolate ${NAME}; \ escapes the next character (\$, \", \\; in double quotes also \n, \t).
    • Single-quoted text is literal: no escapes, no interpolation.
    • A $ not followed by { is literal.

Instructions

  • FROM scratch|<base> [AS name] starts a stage. Every instruction except ARG must come after the first FROM; each FROM after that starts a new stage, and COPY/RENDER apply to the most recent one.

    • scratch (bare word; "scratch" is a path) is an empty tree.
    • <base> that is a bare identifier naming an earlier stage starts from a copy of that stage's final tree (Docker-like). Anything else is a context-relative directory, with COPY's sandbox rules (E_PATH_ESCAPE, symlinks inside the context only, .git/export dir skipped); a file is E_TYPE, a missing path E_NOT_FOUND. A stage name wins over a same-named directory; write ./name to force the directory. Files seeded from a directory get the origin Sitefile:<line> FROM; files inherited from a stage keep their original origin.
    • Stage names are identifiers, unique, and share no namespace with ARG/LET/IMPORT: a collision in either order is E_DUPLICATE. A name used before its stage is complete (itself or a later stage) is E_UNDEFINED, so there are no cycles.
    • Scope: stages scope only the tree. ARG, LET and IMPORT stay one global namespace in source order, wherever they appear, and an IMPORT is usable from any later stage.
    • EXPORT is still exactly one and last, and exports from the last stage. Earlier stages exist only to feed later ones.

  • ARG NAME[: string|number|boolean] [= value]. No default means required; --build-arg NAME=value overrides. Unknown --build-arg names are warnings.

  • Build args from files and the environment (CLI):

    • --build-arg-file <path> (repeatable) reads a flat .json object, a flat .yaml/.yml mapping, or a .env file (KEY=value lines, export prefix, # comments, 'literal' or "escaped" quotes). Values must be strings, numbers or booleans. .env files are parsed, never executed: no $VAR or $(…) expansion.
    • --build-arg NAME (no =) takes the value from the environment variable NAME; an unset variable is a usage error.
    • Precedence: Sitefile default < files (later files win) < --build-arg. Each ARG's declared type still applies.

  • LET NAME[: type] = value. ARG and LET share one namespace; rebinding fails.

  • Operands of every instruction can use ${NAME} for ARG/LET names defined on an earlier line. Dotted access is only allowed inside RENDER templates.

  • IMPORT name FROM <uri> [AS file|text|json|yaml|csv|markdown|wbn|tree] [INTEGRITY sha256:<hex>] [SORT BY key [ASC|DESC]]

    • AS markdown and SORT BY: see Markdown and template blocks below; AS yaml, AS csv, AS wbn and directories of data files: see Data files.
    • <uri> is a context-relative path or an https:// URL (http:// only with --allow-http). Other schemes fail with E_PROTOCOL.
    • Default kind: tree for a local directory, otherwise file.
    • text must be valid UTF-8; json must parse. Both produce values: they can be read by RENDER templates but not copied (E_TYPE).
    • AS tree on a file (local or remote) means "extract this archive"; archives are never extracted implicitly. See Archives below. A local directory with AS tree imports the directory as before.
    • Import names must not equal an ARG/LET name or another import.

  • COPY [--overwrite] [--from=<stage>] <source> <dest>

    • With --from=<stage>, <source> is an absolute path (starts with /, no ..) inside the final tree of an earlier, completed stage: /out/ or /a.txt. File, directory, trailing-slash and conflict rules below apply unchanged. A missing path is E_NOT_FOUND; an unknown, current or later stage is E_UNDEFINED (at the flag).
    • Otherwise <source> is a context-relative path, or name: / name:/inner/path for an import. Write ./foo:bar for a local file whose name contains :. A URL source fails: use IMPORT then COPY.
    • <dest> must be absolute.
    • File source: if <dest> ends with /, or already exists as a directory in the tree, the file goes to <dest>/<basename>; otherwise <dest> is the new file's path.
    • Directory source: its contents are placed under <dest>. A trailing slash on either side makes no difference.

  • RENDER [--escape=none|html] [--overwrite] [--from=<stage>] <template> TO <dest> [FOR item IN list]

    • <template> is a source like COPY's (including --from, so a template can be produced by an earlier stage) and must be a UTF-8 file. <dest> is a file path (no trailing slash).
    • Templates use ${NAME} for ARG/LET, ${name} for a text import, and ${name.key.0.key} for a scalar in a JSON import. $${ writes a literal ${. Unknown names fail with the template's line and column.
    • --escape=html escapes & < > " ' in every substituted value.

  • Inline content (heredocs). The source of COPY and the template of RENDER can be written in the Sitefile itself:

    RENDER --escape=html <<HTML TO /index.html
<h1>${TITLE}</h1>
HTML
COPY <<CSS /style.css
h1 { color: teal }
CSS
    • <<NAME (an identifier) must start a word outside quotes, in place of the source operand. The body is every following line up to a line that is exactly NAME; each body line keeps its \n. <<-NAME strips leading tabs from body lines and the closing line.
    • The body is raw: no comments, blank-line skipping, continuations or escapes. A missing closing line, a second << on one instruction, or << anywhere but the source fails with E_SYNTAX; so does combining it with --from.
    • RENDER bodies are templates with the same rules as template files, and errors report the Sitefile line and column. COPY bodies are written byte for byte (no ${} substitution) with mode 0644, to a file destination (E_PATH for a directory). Conflict rules and --overwrite apply as usual.
    • Only COPY and RENDER lines are scanned for <<; elsewhere it is plain text.
    • See examples/inline/.

  • EXPORT <path> [AS directory|zip|tar|tgz|wbn|oci] [BASE <url>] [AT <root>] must be the last instruction, exactly once; it exports from the last stage. The format defaults to directory; tar.gz is accepted as an alias for tgz; names are case-insensitive. BASE (an operand, so ${VAR} works) is the URL the tree is mounted at and is required by wbn (from here or --base-url). With AS oci, BASE is instead a container image to build on (see oci below). --base overrides it. AT (an operand) is the directory the files occupy inside an oci image (default /srv/www; --oci-root overrides it); with any other format it is an error (E_VALIDATION). The CLI's --out picks the host destination and --format / --base-url override the Sitefile's AS / BASE.

  • RUN is rejected: the MVP never runs shell commands.

Markdown and template blocks (see examples/blog/)

  • IMPORT posts FROM ./posts AS markdown reads every .md/.markdown file in a directory (other files are ignored) as a list of documents, in path order; a single file gives one document. A document is its frontmatter fields plus:
    • slug: the file name without the extension and without a leading YYYY-MM-DD-, unless the frontmatter sets slug (letters, digits, ., _, ~, - only, E_VALIDATION otherwise)
    • date: that leading YYYY-MM-DD, unless the frontmatter sets date
    • path, content (the body as HTML) and excerpt (plain text of the first paragraph, about 200 characters), which frontmatter cannot override
  • Frontmatter is a YAML subset between --- lines: key: value scalars (quoted or plain strings, numbers, true/false, null), inline [a, b] and block - a lists. Dates stay strings. Anything else (nested maps, multi-line strings) fails with E_FRONTMATTER at its line.
  • Markdown is a dependency-free subset: ATX/setext headings, paragraphs, hard breaks, fenced and indented code, blockquotes, nested lists, thematic breaks, emphasis, strong, ~~del~~, code spans, links, images and autolinks. Not supported: tables, footnotes, reference links, task lists. Raw HTML is always escaped, and links or images with schemes other than http, https, mailto, relative or # lose their URL.
  • SORT BY key [ASC|DESC] orders documents by a field: numbers and numeric strings numerically, everything else as strings, so ISO dates sort correctly (it also works on other list imports, see Data files). Documents without the field come last; ties keep path order.
  • RENDER … TO <dest> FOR item IN list renders the template once per element of an imported list (markdown documents or a JSON array). The destination may use ${item} / ${item.key}; every resulting path is normalized like any destination, and two elements writing one path fail with E_CONFLICT. The template sees item plus every ARG, LET and IMPORT.
  • Templates support blocks (in addition to ${name} and ${name.key}):
    • ${#each list as item}…${else}…${/each} repeats for each element; the ${else} part renders for an empty list. A missing key such as ${#each post.tags as t} on a post without tags counts as empty.
    • ${#if value}…${else}…${/if} and ${#if !value}: missing, null, false, '', 0 and empty lists are false.
    • ${value|raw} inserts a value without escaping, for ${post.content|raw} under --escape=html. Every other value is still escaped.
    • A block tag alone on its line removes that whole line from the output.
    • Unbalanced blocks, a second ${else} or an unknown |filter fail with E_TEMPLATE at the tag.

Data files: YAML, CSV and Web Bundles (see examples/data/)

All of these are values: templates read them, FOR iterates over them, and they can't be COPY'd (E_TYPE). Parse errors are E_DATA with the file's line and column.

  • AS yaml: a safe YAML subset: nested block mappings and sequences (including lists of mappings), flow […] / {…}, block scalars | / > with chomping, comments, and the same scalars as frontmatter (dates stay strings). Not supported: anchors/aliases, tags, multiple documents, complex keys, merge keys. An empty document is null.
  • AS csv: RFC 4180 (quoted fields, "" escapes, embedded commas and newlines, CRLF, BOM). The header row gives the keys; every row is an object of strings; a row with the wrong number of fields is an error.
  • AS wbn: a Web Bundle (b1 or b2) as data: { version, primaryUrl, entries: [{ url, path, status, contentType, headers, size, content? }] }, entries in URL order. content is the body as text for textual responses (text/*, JSON, XML, JavaScript, SVG) that are valid UTF-8.
  • AS tree on a .wbn file unpacks the bundle into files (detected by its magic bytes, like tar and zip): URL pathnames become paths (…/ → …/index.html), percent-decoded; if the bundle mixes origins each path is prefixed with /<host>. Only status-200 responses become files. Unsafe paths are E_ARCHIVE_UNSAFE; the archive limits apply.
  • A directory imported AS json or AS yaml is a list with one entry per .json / .yaml / .yml file, in path order. An object becomes { slug, date?, path, ...fields } (slug and date from the file name as for Markdown; fields can override them); any other value becomes { slug, path, value }.
  • SORT BY applies to any list import (markdown, json, yaml, csv); the value must be a list of objects. Numbers and numeric strings (such as CSV cells) compare numerically.

Plugins: PLUGIN and TRANSFORM (see docs/PLUGINS.md, examples/motion/)

  • PLUGIN name FROM ./plugins/x.mjs|x.wasm [INTEGRITY sha256:…] declares a renderer: a local .mjs module in its own folder (not the context root), or a WebAssembly module with no imports (anywhere; see docs/PLUGINS.md). URLs fail with E_PROTOCOL. Plugin names share the ARG/LET/IMPORT/stage namespace.

  • TRANSFORM [--overwrite] [--from=stage] [<source>] WITH name TO <dest> [OPTIONS key=value …] [FOR item IN list] sends the source (a file, an inline body, or a value import) and the options to the plugin and writes what it returns: one file at <dest>, or several under <dest>/. Without a source, the plugin gets the FOR element, or only its options. <dest> and option values may use ${item.key}.

  • Plugins run in a separate Node process with --permission: read access to their own folder only; no writes, processes, workers, network or environment; a per-call time limit (--plugin-timeout). Failures are E_PLUGIN. This protects against accidents, not deliberately malicious code: pin plugins with INTEGRITY.

  • TOOL name declares an external program (name is an identifier and the program's file name, e.g. ffmpeg). It runs only if the CLI allows it with --allow-exec name[=/abs/path]; otherwise the build fails with E_UNSUPPORTED naming the flag. Tool names share the namespace above.

  • A TRANSFORM WITH a tool ends with ARGS <argument> … (the rest of the line; so OPTIONS and FOR come first). Each word is one argv entry (quote words that contain spaces); there is no shell. ${…} interpolation applies as in other operands. The host replaces {input} (the source file, written to a temp dir; needs a source), {output} (required: the one file the tool must write, taking its extension from <dest>) and {option.key} (an OPTIONS value). Other braces (such as ffmpeg's %{pts}) are literal. A tool takes a file source (or none, with FOR or alone), and <dest> is a file, not a directory. Failures, timeouts and oversized outputs are E_PLUGIN. See docs/PLUGINS.md.

  • Results are cached between builds (docs/PLUGINS.md, "Caching").

Writes and conflicts

  • Writing a path that already holds identical bytes and mode is a no-op that keeps the first writer as the owner.
  • Writing different content fails with E_CONFLICT naming the first owner, unless the instruction has --overwrite.
  • A file can never replace a directory or the reverse.

Local sources

  • Absolute paths and .. that escapes the context fail with E_PATH_ESCAPE.
  • Symlinks are followed only when their real target stays inside the context; otherwise E_PATH_ESCAPE. Directory symlink cycles are skipped.
  • When copying directories, .git and the export directory (if it is inside the context) are always skipped.
  • Regular files with more than one hard link are refused with E_HARDLINK: realpath cannot tell whether a hard link aliases a file outside the context. --allow-hardlinks (allowHardlinks) permits them; by passing it you assert that every hard-linked file in the context is safe to publish. pnpm hard-links packages from its store into node_modules, so a context that includes a pnpm node_modules needs either .sitefileignore to exclude it (preferred) or --allow-hardlinks. The check applies to files that are actually read (explicit sources and the non-ignored files of a directory walk), so ignored hard links never trigger it.
  • File modes are reduced to 0644 or 0755.

.sitefileignore

An optional file at the context root filters directory walks (COPY ./dir, IMPORT ./dir, ...). It is never applied to a source named explicitly (COPY ./drafts/a.txt /a.txt works even if drafts/ is listed). Syntax is a gitignore subset:

  • Blank lines and # comments are skipped; \# and \! match literal leading characters.
  • !pattern re-includes; the last matching rule wins.
  • A trailing / matches directories only.
  • A leading / or a / in the middle anchors the pattern to the context root; otherwise it matches at any depth.
  • * and ? match within one path segment; a ** segment matches any number of directories. Character classes ([abc]) are not supported.
  • As in gitignore, a file cannot be re-included when a parent directory is excluded: excluded directories are not descended into.
  • Rules do not affect .git and the export directory, which are always skipped. .sitefileignore, Sitefile and Sitefile.lock are not auto-ignored (explicit is better); add them to the file to keep them out of your output. A .sitefileignore that is a symlink must stay inside the context; a dangling one fails the build (E_NOT_FOUND) rather than being skipped, since skipping it could publish files it was meant to exclude.

Remote sources and the lockfile

  • Only https: by default. Credentials in URLs are rejected. Every resolved address must be public unless --allow-private-network (NAT64 addresses are judged by the IPv4 address they embed); the check runs at connect time, so DNS rebinding cannot slip past it. Redirects are followed manually (max 5) and every hop is re-checked.
  • Bodies are capped (--max-download-bytes, default 50 MiB), requested with accept-encoding: identity, and never decompressed or executed.
  • Sitefile.lock (JSON, next to the Sitefile) records each remote URL's sha256 and size. An unpinned URL already in the lockfile must match it (E_LOCK_MISMATCH; rerun with --update-lock). --frozen-lockfile fails instead of adding entries (E_LOCK_MISSING).
  • Library option fetchPolicy.ca (PEM string or Buffer) trusts an extra CA for https in addition to Node's default store (bundled roots plus NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS / --use-system-ca), for tests and enterprise private CAs. Certificate and hostname verification are never disabled; there is no CLI flag for it.

Archives (IMPORT … AS tree on a file)

  • Formats are detected from magic bytes, not names: tar (ustar or v7), tar.gz / tgz (gzip), and zip (stored and deflate; no zip64, no encryption). Anything else fails with E_TYPE. Supported tar extras: POSIX ustar prefix (old GNU headers keep timestamps there and are read without it), GNU long names, pax path/size (a malformed record is E_ARCHIVE). Other pax keys are ignored. Zip directories are recognized by a trailing / or by a directory mode. Decompression is asynchronous, so other imports keep making progress.
  • INTEGRITY and the lockfile apply to the archive bytes exactly as for file imports, and the import's provenance digest is the archive's digest.
  • Directories are implicit. Modes are reduced to 0644/0755. A single top-level directory is not stripped: COPY name:/top/ / does that.
  • Unsafe entries are rejected, never skipped: absolute paths (including C:), .. segments, backslashes, NUL (E_ARCHIVE_UNSAFE), and symlink, hard link, device and fifo entries (E_ARCHIVE_UNSAFE). Duplicate paths, or a file and directory at one path, fail with E_CONFLICT. Malformed or truncated archives fail with E_ARCHIVE.
  • Limits (E_ARCHIVE_LIMIT), configurable through BuildOptions.archiveLimits: maxEntries 10 000, maxTotalBytes 500 MiB of uncompressed content, and maxRatio 100 (uncompressed:compressed, measured on the gzip stream or the whole zip; not enforced below 1 MiB of output, since tar padding compresses extremely well). Inflation is bounded with zlib's maxOutputLength, so a bomb is stopped at the limit, never fully inflated; zip entries are never inflated beyond their declared size. The download cap still applies first.

Export formats

--out is a directory for directory and a file for every other format. Default --out: <context>/dist, dist.zip, dist.tar, dist.tar.gz, dist.wbn. The format is chosen by, in order: --format; the --out extension (.zip, .tar, .tar.gz/.tgz, .wbn), so -o site.zip writes a zip; then the Sitefile's EXPORT ... AS; then directory. .oci.tar selects oci.

All archive writers are deterministic: the same tree gives byte-identical output (for the same Node/zlib version), whatever the order files were added. Entries are sorted by path; there are no directory entries (directories are implicit); uid/gid are 0 with no user/group names; modes are the tree's 0644/0755. Timestamps are fixed: zip uses the DOS epoch 1980-01-01 00:00, tar uses mtime 0, and the gzip header mtime is 0 (OS byte fixed to Unix). If the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH environment variable is set (non-negative integer seconds), it is used for the zip (clamped to 1980..2107, 2-second resolution) and tar timestamps instead.

  • zip: node:zlib raw deflate (stored when deflate does not shrink the entry), CRC-32, central directory, UTF-8 names (flag bit 11), unix modes in the external attributes (version made by = 3 << 8). No zip64: more than 65535 entries, a file of 4 GiB or more, or an archive of 4 GiB or more fails with E_EXPORT.

  • tar: POSIX ustar. A name over 100 bytes is split into prefix/name at a /; if it still does not fit (prefix over 155 bytes, or no usable /), a pax x header carries the full path. Files of 8 GiB or more fail with E_EXPORT.

  • tgz: gzip of that tar.

  • oci: an OCI image (v1.1) of the site's files. The image has one layer: a deterministic tar of the tree placed under the root (default /srv/www, AT/--oci-root; the parent directory entries srv and srv/www are emitted so runtimes can unpack it), gzip-compressed (application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar+gzip). The config's rootfs.diff_ids is the sha256 of the uncompressed tar; the layer descriptor is the sha256 of the gzip. created is SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH or 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z; architecture/os default to amd64/linux (--platform os/arch; metadata only). Labels: org.opencontainers.image.title (the context directory name), dev.sitefile.root, any --label key=value, and, only with --git-labels, .source and .revision from the repository checkout (read from its .git directory without running anything; credentials in URLs are dropped). Git labels are off by default because they change the image ID on every commit even when the files are identical, and finding the checkout reads outside the build context. Build-arg values are never written. The config, manifest and index are canonical JSON (sorted keys, no whitespace), so the same build always yields the same manifest digest. --out ending in .tar (site.oci.tar) is an OCI archive (a tar of the layout, below); any other --out with --format oci is an OCI layout directory: oci-layout, index.json (one manifest entry, annotated org.opencontainers.image.ref.name when you pass -t) and blobs/sha256/<hex>. The image contains only files: it has no entrypoint and is not runnable on its own. Use it as a source of files, e.g. COPY --from=<image> /srv/www /usr/share/nginx/html in a Dockerfile, unless you give it a BASE:

    EXPORT / AS oci BASE docker.io/library/nginx:alpine AT /usr/share/nginx/html (or --base) makes a runnable image. The base (a bare name means Docker Hub) is pulled for the target platform (--platform, default linux/amd64; a base of another platform is E_REGISTRY) into the local store, and the result is: the base's layers, then the site layer. The config is the base's (Entrypoint, Cmd, Env, ExposedPorts, WorkingDir, User, ... preserved) with rootfs.diff_ids and history extended, labels merged (--label and sitefile's own win over the base's), and created kept from the base unless SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set. The site layer is added on top, so it overlays same-named files of the base (nginx's default index.html) but does not delete the others. Docker layer media types are rewritten to their OCI equivalents (same bytes, same digests). The manifest and config record the base as org.opencontainers.image.base.name / .base.digest. An OCI archive or layout export contains the base blobs too, so it loads anywhere (docker load -i site.oci.tar); -t stores the same image in the local store (save, push, serve work: serve serves the site layer). Layers are held in memory while exporting an archive.

    Reproducibility: the output is a pure function of the files, options and the base's manifest digest. Pin the base: BASE nginx:alpine@sha256:... (the Sitefile is the record). For a tag, Sitefile.lock gets an images entry ("docker.io/library/nginx:alpine": {"digest": "sha256:..."}, the digest the tag pointed at, an index for multi-platform images) the first time it is resolved, and later builds fetch by digest and never re-resolve the tag. --frozen-lockfile fails with E_LOCK_MISSING for an unpinned, unlocked tag; --update-lock re-resolves it; --no-lockfile resolves the tag every build and warns. A base already in the store is used without network access. Pulling goes through the same registry client, limits and credentials as sitefile pull (docs/CLI.md); --insecure-registry applies.

  • wbn: an unsigned Web Bundle, format version b2 (draft-ietf-wpack-bundled-responses): top-level CBOR array [magic "🌐📦", version "b2\0\0", section lengths, [index, primary?, responses], 8-byte length], with index entries url => [offset, length]. Checked against the WICG reference reader dump-bundle (a test runs it when it is installed). The CBOR is deterministic (map keys in bytewise order). Decisions:

    • Base URL: required; an absolute https: URL ending in /, with no credentials, query or fragment (E_VALIDATION otherwise). Each file /a/b.css is addressed as <base>a/b.css (path segments percent-encoded).
    • Every index.html is additionally addressed by its directory URL: /index.html as <base> and /docs/index.html as <base>docs/. Both index entries point at the same response.
    • Primary URL: <base>, in a primary section, if /index.html exists; otherwise there is no primary section.
    • Each response has :status 200 and content-type (no other headers). content-type comes from the extension: html/htm, css, js/mjs, json, svg, txt, xml, webmanifest (all with ; charset=utf-8), png, jpg/jpeg, gif, webp, avif, ico (image/x-icon), wasm, woff, woff2, pdf, mp4, webm, mp3; anything else is application/octet-stream.
    • Index entries are [variants-value "", offset, length] where offset is counted from the first byte of the responses section.
    • Not signed, no integrity block, no variants. Layout follows the b2 draft as understood when written; validate with a Web Bundle tool before relying on it in a browser.

File output safety (same rules as directories, plus): --out that is, or contains, the build context, the filesystem root or the home directory is refused (E_EXPORT_UNSAFE); a directory or symlink at --out is E_EXPORT; an existing file outside the context is only replaced with --force (E_EXPORT_UNSAFE). The bytes are written to a temporary sibling (.<name>.sitefile-tmp-<hex>), the parent and destination identity (dev/ino) are re-validated, then it is renamed into place. Only the exact temp file created is ever deleted. The archive is excluded from the build when it lies in the context. Residual risk is the same path-based window as for directories (see below); the single rename is atomic.

Export

  • Output is written to a temporary sibling directory, then swapped in.
  • An existing non-empty destination is replaced only when it is inside the build context, or with --force. A destination that is, or contains, the context is always refused.
  • Race hardening: the exporter records the dev/ino of the destination's parent directory and of the existing destination, creates its temp and backup siblings only in that verified parent, and re-checks everything immediately before the swap (parent real path and identity unchanged, destination still the same real directory and not a symlink, or still absent). Any change aborts with E_EXPORT_UNSAFE. After the swap it confirms the new destination is the directory it wrote, and it deletes the old directory only if its dev/ino matches the one it validated.
  • Residual risk: Node has no openat/renameat2, so checks are path-based and cannot be bound to a directory handle. The two renames (old aside, new into place) are not atomic together, so the destination briefly does not exist. An attacker with write access to the parent can still swap a path between a check and the next rename; this is detected afterwards (the previous output is preserved at the backup path and nothing unvalidated is deleted), not prevented. Renaming onto an originally absent destination that an attacker just created as an empty directory succeeds on POSIX. If the parent directory itself is moved away mid-export, the temp directory moves with it and is left behind. Do not export into directories writable by untrusted users.
